title: Complete Urinalysis Workflow

references.label: CLSI Standards for Clinical Laboratory Practice

purpose: To evaluate a urine specimen across its physical, chemical, and microscopic components as a broad, inexpensive screen of renal function, urinary tract health, and systemic metabolic status.
principle: A complete urinalysis integrates three complementary layers of information: physical examination (color, clarity, specific gravity) reflects concentration and gross composition; chemical (reagent strip) examination screens for substances like glucose, protein, blood, leukocyte esterase, nitrite, ketones, bilirubin, and pH via colorimetric reactions; and microscopic examination of centrifuged sediment directly visualizes cells, casts, crystals, and organisms. No single layer substitutes for the others — for example, a positive chemical blood reaction should be correlated with microscopic red cell findings, since hemoglobin/myoglobin can react on the strip without intact red cells being present.
requiredMaterials: Clean, appropriately labeled urine container (midstream clean-catch, per collection instructions)

procedure.instruction: Examine and record physical characteristics: color, clarity/turbidity, and specific gravity (by refractometer, reagent strip, or urinometer per the laboratory's method).
Mix the specimen well, then dip a reagent strip fully and briefly into the urine, removing excess along the container edge.

procedure.note: Each analyte pad (glucose, protein, blood, leukocyte esterase, nitrite, ketones, bilirubin, urobilinogen, pH, specific gravity) has its own manufacturer-specified read time.
procedure.instruction: Read each pad at its specified time using the color chart or an automated strip reader, following the manufacturer's exact timing — reading too early or late changes results.
Centrifuge a standardized volume of well-mixed urine for the time/speed specified by the laboratory's method; decant the supernatant and resuspend the sediment in the small remaining volume.

Place a drop of resuspended sediment on a slide, coverslip it, and examine systematically under low then high power for cells, casts, crystals, bacteria, and other elements (see the related urine sediment entry).
Correlate all three components (physical, chemical, microscopic) before reporting — discordant findings between layers should prompt review rather than automatic reporting.

observations: Document physical appearance, all chemical strip results, and a systematic count/description of microscopic elements per high-power/low-power field.
interpretation: Urinalysis findings are interpreted together and in clinical context; isolated abnormal findings (e.g. trace protein alone) carry different weight than concordant patterns (e.g. blood + protein + red cell casts, suggestive of a renal source).
precautions: Examine fresh specimens promptly — cells and casts degrade and crystals can form or dissolve on standing, and bacteria can proliferate, all of which distort results if the specimen sits too long before processing.
Use a properly collected specimen (midstream clean-catch or equivalent) to minimize contamination artifacts.
limitations: Reagent strip chemistry has known interferences (e.g. high specific gravity, certain drugs, ascorbic acid) that can cause false positives/negatives — the manufacturer's specific interference list applies, not a generic rule.
Microscopic sediment interpretation requires trained morphologic recognition and standardized reporting (elements per field), and results vary somewhat with concentration technique.
biosafetyNotes: Urine is a biohazard; use standard precautions and dispose of specimens/sediment per biohazard waste protocol.
